Work should be fair, safe and respectful. 
 
The United Workers Union exists to make sure workers aren’t facing problems alone, across 45+ industries, in every state in Australia.
 
If you’ve ever felt like your boss holds all the power, you’re not imagining it. Together, workers change that.

A United Workers Union survey of almost 1,000 early childhood educators found 90% say a lack of inclusion support compromises the safety of all children in their care, while 87% say they are regularly unable to give children the education and care they deserve.
 
For ACT educator Leane Townrow, the problem became impossible to ignore. After working in a for-profit childcare centre, she moved to a not-for-profit service because she became increasingly concerned about what she was seeing.
 
"In my experience, it was never about the educators, the families or the children in the space. It was always about the numbers on the page matching up with their profit needs."
 
When children with additional needs don't receive the support they require, educators are left trying to fill a gap they didn't create.
 
"When the staffing isn't there, educators are left carrying a gap they didn't create, and it's the children, families and educators who rely on these services who bear the cost."—UWU Early Education Director Carolyn Smith.
 
Every child deserves the support they need, and every educator deserves the staffing to provide it.

The workers who make Australia's favourite biscuits have walked off the job today for the first time since the 1990s.
 
More than 160 Arnott's workers in Adelaide are taking 24 hours of protected industrial action after four years of 2.5% annual pay rises have left them 9.5% behind the cost of living.
 
As workers struggle to make ends meet, Arnott's owner KKR manages hundreds of billions of US dollars in assets globally.
 
Workers aren't asking for anything unreasonable. They're standing together for a fair deal that recognises the value of the work they do every day.
 
✊ We stand with Arnott's workers as they fight for fair pay.

Four days. Hundreds of delegates. Countless conversations, ideas and connections.
Here's what some of our members will be taking home from the 2026 UWU Member Convention. ✊

Since April, more than 400 workers from across Queensland have shared their experiences with United Workers Union. Their stories describe being pushed, punched, kicked, spat on, sworn at and having objects thrown at them while simply doing their jobs.

The Department's own figures show occupational violence and aggression was the leading cause of workplace injury in Queensland schools last year, with 20,833 reported incidents, including around 1,000 requiring medical treatment or hospitalisation.

Teacher Aides and School Cleaners have spoken. Minister John-Paul Langbroek must now deliver the action, staffing and support needed to make Queensland schools safer for everyone.

That’s a wrap for the 2026 United Workers Union Member Convention!
 Over four days, delegates from across the country came together to share experiences, learn from each other and help shape the future direction of our union.
 Today, delegates brought the work of Convention together, reporting back, making decisions and discussing how we take our agenda forward.
 Our union is strongest when members across industries, workplaces and communities stand together.
 Delegates are heading home with new ideas, stronger connections and a shared commitment to keep organising and building power.
 Thank you to every delegate who travelled, participated, shared their experiences and helped make Convention happen.
 Now it’s time to take that energy back to our workplaces and keep building a stronger union together. ✊

Day three of the United Workers Union Member Convention was about building our power. 
 
Delegates began the day hearing from First Nations members and Thomas Mayo about building power, solidarity and a stronger union.
 
Across a full day of workshops, delegates shared experiences, developed skills and worked together on how we organise, campaign and build power in our workplaces, industries and communities.
 
The ideas and discussions from workshops were brought back to the Convention floor as delegates shared what they had learned and how we can put it into action.
 
There’s one more day to go. Tomorrow, delegates will bring the work of Convention together and discuss how we take our agenda for a stronger union forward. ✊

Occupational violence isn't always physical.

For many Queensland Teacher Aides and School Cleaners, it's the daily verbal abuse, threats and intimidation that leave lasting impacts.

The Crisafulli Government promised action, but workers haven't seen the extra staff, funding or workplace changes they were promised.

It's time for Minister John-Paul Langbroek to deliver practical action to make Queensland schools safer for workers and students.
